results.note: Rendered pp. 1343-1344 (Table 2-3 at 300 dpi): groups, ages, other drugs, Table 3 counts, Mann-Whitney and no-correlation statements, quadriradials (B, E, G) and interchanges (IV, D) match. Person-first rewording faithful. Exact 4-vs-4 minimum two-sided P 2/70 = 0.029 recomputed.

results.corrected_extracted: Cross-sectional comparison, undertaken to test the earlier report of more breaks in cultured cells and in one patient (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967): 8 volunteers who reported taking LSD-25, an estimated 4 to 200 times, and 9 volunteers who had not taken it, said to be selected at random from volunteer groups by a method not described; one 5-ml blood sample each, the samples given random numbers and processed blind; 72-hour cultures; 200 metaphases classified per person; no sample from before LSD use. Some of the LSD group had also taken several doses of cannabis (printed with mescaline or peyote in brackets, as if the same drug), psilocybin or DMT, or combinations of the three, in numbers not given. None of the LSD group had x-ray treatment or diagnostic x-rays within several months of sampling; of the controls, one had had about ten x-ray treatments for acne 22 years earlier and one seven diagnostic x-rays of the head and neck 1 to 2 months before.
results.note: Wording only, no number changed. Printed list: cannabis with mescaline or peyote in brackets, then psilocybin or DMT, and combinations of the three; the anchor split it into four drugs. Everything else matches p. 313 at 300 dpi.

Tables 1-2 match; Table 1 counts give every Table 2 rate. Recomputed: 23.6 vs 11.9, 11.7 (Welch 3.7-19.7), Mann-Whitney P 0.009, 22.3% vs 11.1%, 9.4, 5 of 8. Review: 23.4 vs 11.0 (p. 432), 11.9 (Table 2, p. 433).

Spearman 0.86, 0.48, 0.42, -0.28 reproduce; review p. 433 statement confirmed. Minor: the paper calls amounts and numbers of doses estimates but does not say how timing was obtained; calling timing a self-estimate is an inference.

results.corrected_extracted: Cross-sectional comparison of cultured white blood cells from 22 people who had taken LSD (Table 1) or been exposed to it before birth (Table 2), 6 patients taking various other drugs but no LSD (Table 3) and 14 drug-free controls (Table 4); results given once per person (blood from several people was cultured on two separate occasions) and none from before LSD. Two replicate blood samples per person were collected and coded by one author; cultures and slides were made in another laboratory, and the coded slides were sent to Buffalo, where workers not involved in scoring chose fifty well-spread metaphases per cover slip, on 4 to 6 cover slips per person, and one person scored them. How the patients, the controls and the children were found, and where the patients' LSD came from, are not reported.
results.note: Not stated that each person was sampled once: the same paragraph says blood from several people was cultured on two separate occasions (successive cultures of cases 1 and 19 combined in Tables 2 and 4). Rest confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Breaks per 100 cells (breaks over cells scored): 18 patients with a history of LSD, 12 men and 6 women aged 19 to 52, 5.3 to 25.1, in all 566 breaks in 4282 cells (13.2), all white and all with a history of other drugs or medicines (amphetamines, marijuana, other hallucinogens, phenothiazines, opiates, barbiturates or cocaine), 2 taking chlorpromazine when sampled, the last LSD 2 weeks to 8 months before; 12 drug-free controls 2.0 to 5.5, in all 102 breaks in 2674 cells (3.8), after 2 of 14 controls with 31.0 and 14.0 were left out because a viral infection with high fever and diarrhoea began within 24 hours of sampling. The authors call the increase more than three times the control mean and highly significant, without a test, and report no apparent relation of the break rate with the number or size of doses, the time since the last dose, or the type or number of other drugs; 12 dicentrics and 5 exchange figures were seen in the LSD group and none in the controls. Editors' calculations: per-person means 13.2 against 3.9, a difference of 9.3 breaks per 100 cells (Welch 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3; Mann-Whitney P < 0.001); 16 of 18 above the highest control and 2 within the control range; with the two controls left out included, the controls' per-person mean is 6.5 (pooled, 161 breaks in 2974 cells, 5.4) and the difference in per-person means 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7); amphetamines in 15 and phenothiazines in 10 of the 18.
results.note: Number corrected: with all 14 controls the per-person mean is 6.5, not 5.4 (5.4 is the pooled rate 161/2974); 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7) is the per-person difference (pooled difference would be 7.8). All other figures recomputed and confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Six patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (Table 3): three taking chlorpromazine up to the day of sampling, 17.4, 21.5 (a woman who had also used marijuana for 10 years) and 13.7 breaks per 100 cells; a man with a history of amphetamines, opiates, marijuana and barbiturates, 9.0; a 9-year-old boy taking diphenhydramine, 10.0; and a 9-year-old boy recently given chlorpromazine, thioridazine and diphenhydramine, who had been exposed to opiates throughout pregnancy, 4.0. The authors include this group because most people who take LSD also take other drugs; they say the patients receiving chlorpromazine had a marked increase and were taking it at the time of testing, that 8 of the 18 LSD patients had no phenothiazines yet had raised rates, and that a combined effect cannot be judged; they do not compare this group with the LSD group. Editors' calculation: mean of the six rates 12.6 (161 breaks in 1361 cells, 11.8 per 100), no different from the 18 LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84; difference -0.6, 95% interval -7.3 to 6.1) and higher than the 12 controls (P = 0.008). The 1971 review presents the comparison as made by Cohen et al. and says 12.6 and 13.2 did not differ significantly, naming no test (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 434); the editors' calculation bears this out, but the paper itself reports neither the 12.6 mean nor any comparison or test, and the group was mostly patients taking medicines, two of them children.
results.note: Numbers confirmed. Corrected attribution: the review says Cohen et al. compared the groups, so it does not present the comparison as its own; it names no test. Added case 16's marijuana, case 23's prenatal opiates, and current chlorpromazine.

Table 2 at 300 dpi: ages, sexes, counts (57/300, 39/300, 15/200, 8/200; 119/1000) and other drugs match; timing and low doses (Results, 3rd paragraph); no abnormalities noted and transplacental reading (Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs) confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Cells in a dish, not people: white blood cells from 6 healthy donors, cultured separately and the results pooled for each condition, with LSD added at 0.001 to 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours of culture: 7.7 to 17.5 breaks per 100 cells across the 15 conditions against 3.9 in untreated cultures (65 breaks in 1680 cells), with 11.2 at the lowest concentration and shortest exposure (65 in 578); no statistical test of treated against untreated rates is given. Table 5's footnote calls these figures percentages of cells with breaks, and the text calls the control figure a percentage of cells with abnormalities, but the treated counts sum to the 1009 breaks distributed in Table 6, so they are breaks. Mitosis was 6.2% in controls and lower in every treated culture, more so with longer exposure. The authors take the similarity of the patients' mean rate to the rates at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as a sign that these are the concentrations cells meet in the body, although all five concentrations gave similar rates. Editors' calculations: 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0); the highest rate falls at a different concentration for each exposure time, so there is no concentration-response over a 10,000-fold range; the 1971 review lists 8725 treated cells for this study and calls the increase at the lowest concentration significant (Dishotsky et al., 1971, pp. 431–432). Every condition has more cells and breaks than in the laboratory's earlier report, with the highest rate at the same concentrations, consistent with the earlier cultures being pooled here, which the paper does not say.
results.corrected_locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1044); Figure 2 (p. 1044); Table 5 (p. 1046); Table 6 (p. 1047); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1047, left column)
results.note: Wording only. Cultures were per donor and the data pooled, not the cells. Table 5's footnote calls the figures % of cells with breaks; Table 6 (930 + 79 = 1009) shows they are breaks; the anchor should say so.

results.corrected_extracted: Case 37 of Table 1 is a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells (13.0 per 100). The paper presents itself as extending two preliminary reports, the authors' own earlier one and Irwin and Egozcue's (its refs. 2 and 3), with more in vitro findings and a larger sample of patients, but does not say whether case 37 is the earlier report's single patient. Editors' comparison with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967, p. 1418): that patient was a man of 51 with paranoid schizophrenia, given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy and sampled 8 months after the last session, who had also been treated with chlorpromazine (a phenothiazine) and chlordiazepoxide, with 12 percent breakage in 200 cells. Sex, number of treatments, interval and phenothiazine treatment match; the age differs by a year and the number of cells scored by 100. If he is the same man, the 1971 review counts him twice: as the one patient of that earlier report, which it counts among the positive studies of pure LSD (text, p. 435; Table 3, p. 433, a one-person row with 200 cells, 12.00% breaks and 8 months, printed with reference number 48), and among the 18 people of this study it lists as exposed to illicit LSD (Table 2, p. 433).
results.note: Identity borne out as a possibility. Corrected: the paper extends refs. 2 and 3 (also Irwin and Egozcue); the review's Table 3 has other positive pure-LSD people (refs. 28, 50), so he is not its single one.

key_findings.correction: Some of the LSD group had also taken several doses of cannabis (printed with mescaline or peyote in brackets, as if the same drug), psilocybin or DMT, or combinations of the three; the number of people and the amounts are not reported, and no other drugs, alcohol, tobacco or medicines are reported for either group.

risk_of_bias.note: Design cross-sectional and ROBINS-E agreed; overall high agreed. Post-exposure interventions 'low' rests only on nothing being reported; it does not change the overall judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal wording and a four-dose threshold from one person, cancer links without cancer data.

missed: The authors themselves say the Ph1 chromosome is thought to be absent from lymphoid cells (p. 314, Text, 7th paragraph), so Ph1-like chromosomes in cultured lymphocytes are not the leukaemia marker itself; key finding 9 and the interpretation gap should say so.

cannot_establish says the source and content of the LSD are the participants' estimates; the paper does not state the source at all; only the amounts and the number of occasions are given as estimates.

key_findings.correction: Table 3, six patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD: three taking chlorpromazine up to the day of sampling, 17.4 (34 in 195), 21.5 (43 in 200; this woman had also used marijuana for 10 years) and 13.7 (28 in 205) breaks per 100 cells; a man with a history of amphetamines, opiates, marijuana and barbiturates, 9.0 (18 in 200); a 9-year-old boy taking diphenhydramine, 10.0 (26 in 261); and a 9-year-old boy given chlorpromazine and thioridazine until a month before sampling and diphenhydramine in the last week, born with opioid dependence after exposure throughout pregnancy, 4.0 (12 in 300). The authors say the patients receiving chlorpromazine showed a marked increase and were taking it at the time of testing, that 8 of the 18 LSD patients had no phenothiazines and still showed raised rates, that a combined effect of the two drugs cannot be judged, and that controlled studies of chlorpromazine are in progress. Note: editors' calculation as printed (12.6; 161 in 1361, 11.8; P = 0.84; -0.6, -7.3 to 6.1; P = 0.008). The paper reports neither comparison; the 1971 review presents the comparison as Cohen et al.'s and calls 12.6 and 13.2 not significantly different without naming a test (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 434).

In vitro, Table 5 (separate cultures from 6 donors, the results pooled for each condition because, the authors say without data, the donors did not differ significantly from each other or by sex): breaks per 100 cells after 48 hours 12.6, 7.7, 17.5, 10.7 and 12.5 at 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml; after 24 hours 11.5, 15.8, 13.0, 15.4 and 10.8; after 4 hours 17.1, 10.6, 13.1, 15.2 and 11.2 (65 breaks in 578 cells at 0.001 µg/ml); untreated cultures 3.9 (65 in 1680). The text calls the lowest treated rate almost twice the control and the highest over four times; no test is reported. Most aberrations were chromatid and isochromatid breaks, with a few chromatid exchanges and dicentrics and no rings. (Note unchanged.)

Case 37 in Table 1 is a man of 52 with 15 doses of LSD, the last 8 months before sampling, phenothiazines as his only other drug, and 13.0 breaks per 100 cells (39 in 300). The paper does not say whether he is the patient of its ref. 2; it presents itself as extending the observations of two preliminary reports, its ref. 2 and Irwin and Egozcue's (ref. 3), with additional in vitro findings and a significant sample of patients. (Note unchanged; confirmed against Cohen, Marinello and Back, 1967, pp. 1417-1418.)

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The group taking other drugs but no LSD is presented as exposed to the kinds of drugs LSD patients take (p. 1047), but five of the six had been taking medicines up to or shortly before sampling (chlorpromazine in four, thioridazine in one, diphenhydramine in two), two of them boys of 9; the one woman, taking chlorpromazine, had also used marijuana for 10 years, and only one man had a history of several non-medical drugs (Table 3); the group is not compared with the LSD group, whose rates were similar. | consequence: The paper's own data do not separate LSD from other drugs and medicines; the comparison is left to the reader and was later presented by the 1971 review, as Cohen et al.'s, without a stated test.

risk_of_bias.note: Design cross-sectional (with an in vitro part) and ROBINS-E agreed. Very high for confounding is defensible given the similar rates of the other-drug group; high would also be defensible (six people, mostly on chlorpromazine); overall very high either way.

interpretation_gap.note: Severe: causal wording from a confounded cross-sectional comparison, and leukaemia, birth defects and germ-cell damage none of which was measured.

missed: design_detail says one sampling time per person; the paper does not say so: blood from several people was cultured on two separate occasions (p. 1044), and successive cultures were combined in Tables 2 and 4 (cases 1 and 19, p. 1047). Key finding 0 already says specimens were cultured twice.

analysis.effect_sizes pairs the pooled rate of all 14 controls (5.4, 161 in 2974) with the per-person-mean difference 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7); with all 14, the per-person control mean is 6.5 (pooled difference 7.8).

The Summary (p. 1049) says aberrations were raised, particularly dicentrics, although the results describe only a few dicentrics in vitro and 12 in the LSD group, with chromatid and isochromatid breaks the vast majority (pp. 1044, 1046); the interpretation gap could note this emphasis.
